trait_description: The material density of coral skeleton. Porosity measurements can be converted to density by multiplying the reciprocal of porosity by the maximum density of aragonite (2.94 g cm^-3).
The concentration of MgCO3 in sclerites
Whether species have calcareous sclerites or not. The presence or absence of calcareous sclerites determines some of the most important features of octocorals skeletons
The type of skeleton present in a given octocoral species. Categories were selected based on McFadden et al. 2022
Whether a species has an axis or not. The presence or absence of an internal axis determines one of the most important features of octocorals skeletons
The CaCO3 polymorph present in sclerites (mostly calcite but Aragonite and Vaterite in some species)
The concentration of CaCO3 in sclerites
The Ca/Mg ratio in sclerites
For species with axis only. The concentration of CaCO3 in the axis
A mechanical property of materials that measures the  stiffness when the force is applied lengthwise
The Mg/Ca ratio in sclerites
The CaCO3 polymorph found in the skeleton, without considering sclerites
For species with axis only. The concentration of Mg in axis
For species with axis only. The concentration of MgCO3 in axis

The rigidity of a coral colony or individual, based on the type of skeleton. Allowed values are:  Soft (i.e., species with just a hydrostatic skeleton in which the whole colony is capable of retracting or deflating or greatly changing its volume), Semi-rigid (i.e., species with an axis in which the colony itself is not capable of retraction/deflation) and rigid (i.e., species with a totally hard skeleton that is heavily calcified).
Red list categories as specified by the IUCN Red list of Threatened Species
The water depth at which a coral trait was measured.
Water temperature is a contextual trait of the environment in which a coral trait is measured.
The year in which an observation took place. The month or season in which an observation took place should be added separately.
The month of the year in which an observation took place. The year in which an observation took place should be added separately (Trait ID: 174).
The concentration of dissolved oxygen in the water
The concentration of phosphate oxygen in the water
The salinity of the water
If measurements were taken of a bleached colony
The type of branch (new) or (old) can affect the growth rate
The number of branches that have been clipped in a colony to simulate mortality, which potentially affects growth rates
The order of the branch may affect growth rate
Pollution may affect growth rates of species
Flow rate is a contextual trait of the environment in which a coral trait is measured.
In organisms with determinate modular growth, the age of branches may influence their growth
The silicate concentration in the water.
The water pH.
Whether measurements were taken in a previously harvested site or colony
The habitat type in which the measurements were taken
Whether measurements were taken in female, male or hermaphroditic colonies
Whether a site in which trait measurements were taken was unprotected or protected (e.g., MPA).
The ID given to a colony whose traits have been measured
This contextual trait specify if the trait measurements were taken in an impacted or unimpacted location by oil spills.
The years that have happened since harvest of the coral colonies
In species with polyp dimorphism/trimorphism or axial/lateral colony configuration, the type of polyp that has been measured/examined.
The season of the year in which a trait was measured
The total number of polyps in a colony
The concentration of preys within the water
The date on which a trait was measured
The period of the day in which a trait was measured
Whether the reef in which a trait was quantified was in a healthy or disturbed condition
The minimum (shallowest) observed depth of a species. Data are a mix of individual-level local observations and species-level global estimates based on expert opinion.
The maximum (deepest) observed depth of a species. Data are a mix of individual-level local observations and species-level global estimates based on expert opinion.

Preferred hydrodynamic exposure environment. Derived from preferred habitat textual descriptions, mostly from Veron and Stafford-Smith (2002), Diaz and Madin (2011) and Fabricius and Alderslade, 2001.
Preferred water clarity environment. Derived from preferred habitat textual descriptions, mostly from Veron and Stafford-Smith (2002), Diaz and Madin (2011) and Fabricius and Alderslade, 2001
The depth at which a type specimen (typicaly the holotype) was collected.
Some soft octocoral species can contract at the colony level
The depth zone in which a species is found. Accepted depth zones are: shallow (0 to 50 m), moderately deep (51 to 200 m) and deep (>200 m)
The mechanism used by each octocoral species to obtain food.
Food sources of octocoral species
The size of the preys of a coral
The light zone where the species can be found, in relation to depth. Accepted light zones are photic (0-30 m depth), mesophotic (31 to 150 m depth) and aphotic (>150 m depth).
The ocean basin in which a species is found. Indian and Pacific Oceans are grouped as "pacific."
The climatic zone where an octocoral species can be found. Species can have multiple climatic zones associated.

The marine realm (as defined by Spalding et al. 2007) in which a species can be found. Caution should be taken when using these data, especially when derived from online platforms such as OBIS, where not all observations have been verified to match correct species.

The marine province (as defined by Spalding et al. 2007) in which a species can be found. Caution should be taken when using these data, especially when derived from online platforms such as OBIS, where not all observations have been verified to match correct species.
Whether mature individuals of a species are colonial, solitary or either colonial or solitary (both).
The number of polyps per length or area units.
The size of a colony. Typically associated with a trait that is expected to vary with colony size. The default is planar projected area.

The growth form of a coral colony measured in the field or during an experiment. The range of growth form categories is not constrained (i.e., growth forms should be named as they were in the original resource or dataset), and therefore the number of categories will become large.
The height of a coral colony (or individual) from the bottom to the top.
The width of a coral colony (or individual).
Diameter of the basal trunk in octocorals, including both axis skeleton and tissue. For simplicity, we use the word trunk to refer also to stems, stalks and rods.
The length of the polyp tentacles
The number of pinnules in octocoral tentacles
The projected area when seen from the side, perpendicular to the main growth direction of the colony
For those species with axis, the diameter of the axis skeleton
The length of the rachis in sea pens
The length of the peduncle in sea pens

The height of the polyp (sometimes referred as length). Different authors give different measurements and proxies for this trait (e.g., some report the size of the contracted polyps, whereas others report the size of the entire polyp, including tentacles). In some cases, this information is not given. Number of measured replicates is often lacking as well. Thus, observation notes in the database and original sources should be checked when using this trait for comparative analyses among species.
In octocorals species with calyces, the height of the calyx that contains the polyp
calyces, the diameter of the calyx that contains the polyp
The branching pattern in branched colonies
If the colony has one type of polyp or more (e.g., autozooids and siphonozooids)
In a branched colony, the diameter of branches
The number of tentacles per polyp
Whether polyps can retract into the choenenchyme or not

Growth forms of octocorals coarsely categorized by Fabricius & Gómez-Gras. This trait is a sub-classification of the Type of growth trait into broad groups depending on basic morphological features such as the presence of stem/stalk, the presence of stolons, lobes…etc.
In species with polyp whorls, the number of polyps found per whorl
In species with polyp whorls, the diameter of the polyp whorl
How polyps are distributed within the colony
In sea pens with polyp leaves, the number of polyps in each polyp leave
The distance between two polyps in a coral colony. Typically measured as the distance between the centers of the two polyps (or calyces)
For sea pens only. Whether a species has polyp leaves or not
For sea pens only. Whether a species has a symmetrical rachis or not.
The number of polyp whorls or polyp pairs per length unit

The diameter of the polyp. Different authors give different measurements and proxies for this trait (e.g., some report the size of the contracted polyps, while others report the size of the entire polyp, including tentacles or do not specify it). Thus, observation notes in the database and original sources should be checked when using this trait for comparative analyses among species.
A geometrical index of colony complexity based measures of the change in rugosity with changing scale of measurement

The type of growth of coral species in terms of the main way of space occupation and branching (i.e., erect branched, erect unbranched, massive, horizontal unbranched, horizontal branched and/or solitary/pseudo-solitary). Categories were defined by K.E., Fabricius and D. Gómez-Gras

A sub-classification of the trait Growth form_basic, in which the coarsely classified growth forms of that trait are further subdivided into more detailed categories (K.E. Fabricius and D. Gómez-Gras)
Is the species zooxanthellate?

Typically, the yearly extension for branching and massive corals, or simple linear extension. Growth rate is sometimes measured using different dimensions (e.g., diameter and radius) or over shorter periods of time (e.g., month), which are indicated by measurement standards and methodologies, and so values may need to be standardised before comparisons among measurements can be made.
The rate at which calcium carbonate (e.g., aragonite or calcite) is laid down per unit of skeletal surface area. When using this data, be aware that this trait is measured in numerous ways

The genetic identity of Symbiodinium found in coral tissue at the clade level (broad level of major symbiont taxa). This is typically identified using regions of the nuclear ribosomal DNA, but other regions are also used.
The distance from the external surface to the internal surface of the coral tissue.
The age of the colony at the time of measurement and/or dead.
The life-expectancy of a given species
Defined as ratio of net oxygen produced: oxygen produced by photosynthesis (P) to oxygen released in total ecosystem respiration (R)
The capture rate of coral colonies/individuals
The number of symbionts per polyp or unit surface
The rate of oxygen production measured in the light per unit of skeletal surface area. This includes oxygen consumption due to light respiration.
The rate of oxygen consumption measured in the darkness per unit of skeletal surface area. Values may include both light enhanced dark respiration and dark acclimated dark respiration.
For species with axis only. The radial growth rate of the axis.
Each polyp of the population having gametes of only one sex (either male or female) at maturity (gonochore)

The mode of larval development classified as either a brooder, where fertilization is internal and colonies release planulae larvae, broadcast spawner, where gametes are release for external fertilization and the planulae develops in the plankton, or surface brooder, where gametes are released before fertilization, but remain in the colony surface of the female until they are fertilized and brooded
The diameter of mature oocytes in a population. Determined by histology or dissection or measuring the size of eggs once released from the colony in broadcast spawners.
The number OR VOLUME of eggs (oocytes) OR LARVAE in a polyp.
The colony size, typically diameter or height at which a coral is observed to start producing gametes and reproducing
The age at which a coral is observed to start producing gametes and spawning.
The swimming speed, typically the maximum, of coral larvae.
The size of eggs or planula larvae on release.
Colony fecundity can be estimated in different ways, such as the sum of egg and testes volume per polyp multiplied by the total number of polyps, or by estimating the number of eggs per colony.
The date a coral colony was observed to spawn.
The length of the larvae
The width of the larvae
The duration of the planktonic phase in larvae
The breeding and/or spawning period of a coral
Whether species reproduce following annual cycles or in a continuous manner
The mode of asexual reproduction observed in a species, if any
The duration of the oogenic cycle. For stony corals, this trait appears as length oogenic cycle max.
The duration of the spermatogenic cycle
The number of oocytes per surface unit
The dry weight of holobiont tissue, typically reported as mass per unit of skeletal surface area of a colony.
